title: Riteish Deshmukh Directed a Film About Shivaji Maharaj. It Just Became the Highest-Grossing Marathi Film in History. Every NRI From Maharashtra Needs to Know What's Happening to Regional Cinema.
excerpt: Raja Shivaji has crossed ₹110 crore worldwide in 22 days, dethroning Sairat's decade-long record. It's the first Marathi film to ever cross ₹100 crore. And it's Riteish Deshmukh's directorial debut.
body:
For a decade, Sairat owned the Marathi box office. Nagraj Manjule's raw, devastating love story from 2016 had earned ₹110 crore worldwide, and no Marathi film had come within striking distance. It seemed unbreakable.

It took Riteish Deshmukh — actor, producer, and now first-time director — exactly 22 days to break it.

*Raja Shivaji*, the historical epic about Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, has crossed ₹110 crore worldwide, making it the highest-grossing Marathi film of all time and the first ever to breach the ₹100 crore mark at the Indian box office.

## The Record in Numbers

The breakdown tells an interesting story. The original Marathi version has grossed over ₹76 crore — impressive, but technically still below Sairat and Baipan Bhari Deva (₹90.50 crore) in the core Marathi market. What pushed Raja Shivaji past the finish line was its Hindi dubbed version, which contributed roughly ₹29 crore. Add ₹4.20 crore from overseas, and you're looking at ₹110+ crore worldwide against a ₹75 crore budget.

It's profitable, but here's the nuance: Pinkvilla's analysis points out that in Maharashtra alone — the market that matters most for Marathi cinema — Raja Shivaji likely won't hit ₹100 crore. Films about Shivaji Maharaj in Hindi, like *Tanhaji* (adjusted to ₹250 crore today) and *Chhaava* (₹300+ crore in Maharashtra), have done significantly better in the same territory.

The record is real. The dominance is qualified. But the milestone is historic.

## What Makes It Work

Riteish Deshmukh didn't just act in the film — he directed it, his first time behind the camera. That alone made it an event. He plays Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj with an intensity that even sceptical critics have acknowledged, and the supporting cast reads like a who's-who of Indian cinema: Abhishek Bachchan, Sanjay Dutt, Vidya Balan, Sachin Khedekar, Mahesh Manjrekar, and Bhagyashree (who plays Rajmata Jijabai, earning praise for portraying a character older than the actress who plays her son).

Released on Maharashtra Day — May 1 — the timing was strategic. The film opened to ₹13.85 crore worldwide on its first day, a Marathi cinema record. The opening weekend hit ₹41.65 crore, another record. The first-week numbers were strong, though the second and third weeks showed the kind of decline that separates "big hit" from "all-time phenomenon."

The word-of-mouth has been mixed. Some viewers found the pacing uneven; others praised the battle sequences and emotional beats. What's indisputable is that enough people bought tickets to make history.

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

Here's why this matters beyond Maharashtra.

First, the ₹100 crore barrier. Marathi cinema has been producing acclaimed films for decades — *Court*, *Sairat*, *Natsamrat*, *Baipan Bhari Deva* — but none had crossed the psychological century mark in India. *Raja Shivaji* just did. That changes the economics of what Marathi producers can greenlight. When the ceiling rises, so do budgets, ambitions, and the quality of talent willing to bet on regional cinema.

Second, the crossover. The Hindi dubbed version earning ₹29 crore is significant. It proves that a Marathi-language historical can find audiences across India, not just in Maharashtra. This is the Baahubali effect applied to Marathi cinema: make it big enough, and language barriers dissolve.

Third, the subject matter. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj is not just a historical figure — he's a cultural icon for millions of Maharashtrians worldwide. For NRIs in the US, UK, Australia, and the Gulf who grew up hearing stories of the Maratha warrior king, a ₹75 crore theatrical film about his life — shot with production values that can compete with mainstream Bollywood — is a cultural event.

## The Bigger Picture

*Raja Shivaji* arrives in a year where regional cinema is quietly having a moment. Drishyam 3 from Malayalam has crossed ₹117 crore worldwide in just four days. Suriya's Tamil film Karuppu is heading toward ₹250 crore. Telugu cinema continues to produce ₹300+ crore grossers with regularity.

Hindi cinema, for all its attention and star power, is increasingly just one player in a multi-language industry. *Raja Shivaji*'s record confirms what the data has been showing for years: India's film industry isn't "Bollywood plus others." It's a constellation of industries, each with its own stars, audiences, and now its own century-club members.

## Where It Stands

*Raja Shivaji* is likely to finish its theatrical run around ₹115-120 crore worldwide. It won't reach ₹150 crore — the second-weekend slowdown made that clear. But it doesn't need to. It broke the record. It crossed ₹100 crore. And it proved that Marathi cinema can play at a scale that was unthinkable five years ago.

For Riteish Deshmukh, it's a vindication — as a director, as a Maharashtrian, and as someone who bet ₹75 crore on a story about his hero. The first century in Marathi cinema belongs to him.
nri_angle: For Marathi NRIs worldwide, Raja Shivaji isn't just a film — it's a cultural milestone. The first Marathi film to cross ₹100 crore proves that regional Indian cinema can compete at scale. The Hindi dubbed version alone crossed ₹29 crore, signalling genuine crossover appeal.
